case.label: C
case.text: Adding more VPN connections to the same virtual private gateway adds more tunnels, and with BGP and different prefixes per tunnel the company could spread nightly load by hand. It fails because a virtual private gateway does not do ECMP across tunnels, so one path carries a given prefix, and the manual split is not scalable.

case.label: A
case.text: A Site-to-Site VPN backup over the internet survives the loss of a whole Direct Connect location, so it covers the stated failure modes at low cost. It loses because it is not the MOST resilient design: it adds an internet path with lower and variable capacity, and no second Direct Connect location or second device.

case.label: B
case.text: Transit gateways in both Regions with a transit virtual interface reach both VPCs and scale to more VPCs later. It loses on overhead: it needs two transit gateways, a Direct Connect gateway that the option never mentions, and extra routing, while a Direct Connect gateway with virtual private gateway associations does the job directly.

case.label: B
case.text: An OpenVPN server on EC2 can also use a SAML 2.0 identity provider and reach private subnets. It loses because the stem asks for a fully managed solution with the least overhead, and this option adds patching and scaling work.

case.label: B
case.text: A LAG of two 10 Gbps connections gives 20 Gbps and survives the loss of one connection, so it could carry the full 10 Gbps load. It loses for HIGHEST availability because both links end at one Direct Connect location, so a location failure removes the whole path.

case.label: C
case.text: A second VPN connection from a new customer gateway device removes the single device as a point of failure and so gives stronger high availability. It loses on the least-overhead constraint: the existing connection already has a second tunnel that is simply not configured, and configuring it fixes the update outage with far less work.

case.label: D
case.text: A software VPN appliance on EC2 with IPsec over the internet also meets the one-week and encryption needs and the router supports IPsec. It loses because the managed Site-to-Site VPN gives the same result without running, patching or scaling an instance.

case.label: A
case.text: TLS in every application does encrypt the application data in transit and needs no change to the virtual interface. It loses because the rule says all traffic on the connection, which TLS in each application does not guarantee, and changing every application is far more work than one network-level fix.

case.label: B
case.text: A Site-to-Site VPN is the cheapest option and 200 Mbps is within what a VPN can carry. It loses because the stem asks for a private line that does not use the internet, and this VPN runs over the internet.

case.label: A
case.text: A new endpoint with split-tunnel turned on, plus routes and rules copied over, would also give the restricted tunnel. It is a valid but wasteful way to get there: every user has to move, which is more overhead than turning split-tunnel on at the existing endpoint.

case.label: B
case.text: A software VPN appliance on EC2 over Direct Connect also gives encrypted, consistent-performance transfers and the router supports IPsec. It loses because the managed Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect achieves the same without an instance to operate.

case.label: C
case.text: IPsec through a Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect encrypts all the traffic and works with a 10 Gbps connection. It loses because IPsec adds header overhead that lowers the MTU, which the stem rules out, and it needs more setup than MACsec.
